pages.text: $(li)The Pixonia Reactor will not melt as long as its net heat output remains negative; monitor heat balance to avoid overheating.$(li)Before activating the MSR, ensure the Net Heat Gen is negative.

Meltdowns occur if Coolant Heater output tanks, Fission Vessel output tanks fill up, or coolant runs out.$(li)A fission reactor controller requires internal cells—no cells = no operation—even with redstone input.
$(li)The Fission Controller is always consumed in a meltdown (along with all cells and half the walls), so it must be passived.

$(li)Use low-conductivity (20%) tubes for the hot fluid (e.g., NaK) and high-conductivity (550%) tubes for the cold fluid (e.g., water) to maximize high-pressure steam production; using 550% tubes for hot NaK reduces efficiency.

$(li)In a Heat Exchanger, water and coolant must flow in opposite directions for proper heat transfer.$(li)Build an HX like an MSR: Frame/Walls/Glass, Controller, Vents, and configured Heat Exchanger Tubes (DISABLED → DEFAULT → PRODUCT OUT → INPUT SPREAD).
$(li)Ensure the heat exchanger is fast enough to process output fluids; if output is blocked, the reactor will melt down and produce free corium.

$(li)A spent polonium molten salt reactor can gain heat when not all fission vessels are active because the center cooler stops working if only one line is partially filled; fully vacate fluid or stop the reactor when the tank is empty.$(li)Running a molten salt reactor at full output can cause it to stop processing;
use logic control (e.g., redstone or automation) to limit fuel input when output tanks exceed a threshold.
$(li)For large corium reactors, avoid placing non-unbreakable blocks directly adjacent to the controller—only corner blocks need to be near it, and walls adjacent to it may randomly melt down.
$(li)Symmetrical neutron source placement (on x, z, and y axes) significantly boosts cooling efficiency; a 5+5 symmetric setup provides ~80% cooling.
